chunks: Common resistor values (E-series). The question: What are some common resistor values?
You cannot buy a resistor of every possible value. Manufacturers make a limited set of standard values called the E-series.
Each value is a fixed percentage bigger than the last (about 21% in the E12 series), so the steps grow as the values grow.
The spacing is set by the part's tolerance, so any value you want is close to a standard one.
Think of shoe sizes. Shops do not stock every possible foot length. They stock sizes spaced so that each one fits a range of feet well enough.
A finer series, like half sizes, fits more closely but means more sizes to stock. Resistor series work the same way.
More values per decade means a closer fit and a tighter-tolerance part.
The more values per decade, the closer you can get to any target. E12/E24/E96 are the points where the grid error matches the usual 10 %, 5 %, 1 % tolerances.
E-series: the standard set of preferred values, such as E12, E24 and E96. The number is how many values per decade.
Decade: a tenfold range, such as 10 to 100 ohms or 1 kilohms to 10 kilohms. Tolerance: how far a real resistor may be from its labeled value, such as 5% or 1%.
Preferred value: a value in a standard series, which is cheap and easy to buy. Voltage divider: two resistors that set a ratio.
E12 has 12 values per decade: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. Say you need 13 kilohms. E12 has no 13, but a 12 kilohms part at 10% may really be anywhere from 10.
8 kilohms to 13. 2 kilohms, so if your design can live with that, it will do. E24 has 13 exactly, with a 5% tolerance. That is the whole idea.
"Resistor values come from the E-series: preferred numbers spaced logarithmically in each decade.
E12 has 12 values and goes with 10 percent parts, E24 has 24 for 5 percent, and E96 has 96 for 1 percent. The spacing makes neighbors overlap within tolerance.
The ones I use constantly are 10, 100, 1k, 4. 7k, 10k, 100k, 1 meg, plus 22 or 33 ohms for series termination.
For dividers I use E96 and then compute the real output with the actual values."
